power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.transformations:
Dichotomous variables will be coded with values of 0 and 1 for ease of interpretation in regression analyses.
Other numerical variables will be centered at the mean in models that test their interaction terms.
Any categorical variables will be dummy-coded where necessary, and the reference group will be clearly defined for each analysis.
table.inference_criteria:
We will follow these guidelines:

1. Significance Testing: 
   - We will report standard errors and confidence intervals to convey the uncertainty around our estimates. When appropriate, we will use p-values to assess statistical significance, with a cut-off of p < 0.05 as the threshold for significance.
   - All tests will be two-tailed, unless a specific directional hypothesis warrants a one-tailed test (none are planned currently).
   
2. Correction for Multiple Comparisons: 
   -When appropriate, we will apply Bonferroni correction or a similar method to adjust for multiple comparisons and reduce the risk of Type I errors.
   
3. Effect Sizes:
   - In addition to p-values, we will report effect sizes (e.g., Cohen’s d for mean differences, R² for regression models) to provide information on the magnitude of observed effects.

4. Model Fit:
   - For regression models, we will assess model fit using R² and adjusted R² values to evaluate how well the model explains the variance in the dependent variable.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will implement two attention checks throughout the survey. Participants who fail both attention checks will be excluded from the analysis. Additionally, we will exclude participants whose survey completion time is either unusually short or excessively long. The average time to complete the survey is approximately 16 minutes. Participants who complete the survey in less than 8 minutes or take longer than 1 hour will be excluded from the dataset. Outliers, in terms of completion time, will be flagged and removed to ensure data quality and consistency.
table.missing_data_handling:
For incomplete or missing data, we will use the following approach:

For participants with limited missing data (i.e., less than 20% of key items), we will consider using appropriate statistical imputation methods - such as multiple imputation - depending on the pattern and extent of missingness. If imputation is not suitable, we will use listwise deletion.

All missing data handling will be clearly documented and reported in the final analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses:
For exploratory analysis, we plan to investigate any additional, unspecified relationships or differences that may emerge from the data. These analyses will include:

1. Unspecified correlations between variables such as personal emotions, emotion norms, and demographic factors that were not initially hypothesized.
   
2. Subgroup analyses based on demographic variables like age, gender, education, or economic status, to see if these factors moderate the relationships between emotion norms, personal emotions, and policy support.
   
3. Interaction effects between multiple predictors that were not originally specified in the hypotheses, such as potential interactions between different emotion norms or between personal emotions and social norms.

4. Exploring trends across countries or conflict groups, looking for differences in the role of emotion norms and personal emotions in policy support that may not have been predicted.

These exploratory analyses will be clearly labeled as such in the final report, and any significant findings will be interpreted cautiously, as they were not pre-specified in the original hypotheses.

table.study_design_overview:
Research Module 1 employs a between-subjects, non-experimental design to examine the relationships between perceived emotion norms, personal emotions, and support for conflict-related policies across thirteen conflict-affected societies. These include seven countries currently experiencing ongoing conflict (Colombia, Ukraine, Ethiopia, Israel, Palestine, Turkey, and India) and six in a post-conflict stage (Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, Serbia, Thailand, and Northern Ireland).

Data will be collected via a cross-sectional online survey administered to a large sample in each country. Samples will aim to be nationally representative - or at least diverse - across key sociodemographic variables, including gender, age, education level, and geographic region. Each participant will respond to measures assessing their personal emotions, perceived group emotion norms, and support for conflict-related policies.

The study targets approximately 1,000 participants per country. In selected countries where preliminary consultations with survey agencies indicate feasibility of sampling from two relevant conflict-affected groups, the target sample size is 2,000 (1,000 from each group). These countries include: Bosnia and Herzegovina (1000 Serbs and 1000 Bosniaks), India (1000 Hindus and 1000 Muslims), Thailand (1000 Thai population and 1000 Malay Muslims), and Northern Ireland (1000 Protestants and 1000 Catholics).

Surveys will be administered in local languages and tailored to the specific context of each conflict-affected society. Local collaborators (researchers with expertise in each context) will assist with survey translation and adaptation to ensure relevance. Survey responses will be anonymous, with informed consent obtained from each participant before they begin.

table.data_collection_procedures:
Data will be gathered through online surveys conducted in 13 conflict-affected societies. Professional survey agencies in each country will be responsible for participant recruitment, survey administration, and data collection.The countries included are divided into two groups based on conflict status:
- Ongoing conflicts: Colombia, Ukraine, Ethiopia, Israel, Palestine, Turkey, and India.
- Post-conflict settings: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, Serbia, Thailand, and Northern Ireland.

Sample Population:
- The target population comprises adults (18 years and older) residing in the selected conflict-affected societies.
- In countries where it is feasible to recruit sufficient numbers of respondents from two distinct conflict-related groups (e.g., Bosnia and Herzegovina, Northern Ireland), samples will include participants from both groups. In these cases, stratified sampling will be used to ensure balanced representation (e.g., Serbs and Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina; Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland). 
- In other contexts, samples will aim to be broadly representative of the general adult population in each country, based on key socio-demographic characteristics such as gender, age, education level, and geographic region.

Recruitment Process:
- Participants will be recruited via professional survey agencies with access to large online participant pools in each country. Agencies will use their established networks of respondents and invite them to participate through email or other online platforms.
- Participants will be asked to complete a 20-minute online survey, and participation will be voluntary.
- Incentives: In line with standard survey practices, participants may receive small compensation, typically in the form of payment or vouchers, provided by the survey agency (e.g., a small cash payment or gift card).

Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria:
- Inclusion Criteria:
  - Participants must be 18 years or older.
  - They must be permanent residents of the conflict-affected country where the survey is being conducted.
  - They should have sufficient language proficiency to understand and complete the survey in the local language.
- Exclusion Criteria:
  - Individuals younger than 18.
  - Participants who do not reside in the conflict-affected region or country being studied.
  - Participants who fail to complete the survey or provide incomplete data will be excluded from the final analysis.
table.sample_size:
The study will analyze data from a total of approximately 16,000 participants across 13 conflict-affected societies. Each country will have a sample size ranging from 1,000 to 2,000 participants, depending on whether the country sample involves one or two distinct conflict groups. In countries with two conflict groups (e.g., Northern Ireland), the sample size will be 2,000, with 1,000 participants per group to allow for comparisons between groups. For countries with only one conflict group, the sample size will be 1,000 participants.

This sample size ensures statistical power for detecting significant relationships between emotion norms, personal emotions, and support for conflict-related policies.
table.sample_size_rationale: We have not conducted a formal power analysis for this study. However, the total number of participants across the 13 conflict-affected societies is expected to exceed 16,000. Our aim is to obtain samples in each country that are either representative or, at minimum, diverse with respect to key socio-demographic characteristics (e.g., gender, age, region, education level). The substantial sample size within each country is intended to ensure sufficient precision in estimating effects and allow for meaningful comparisons across groups and contexts.
table.measured_variables:
1. Outcome Measures:

- Support for Conflict-Related Policies: Participants' support for both conflict-promoting policies (e.g., military aggression, expulsion) and conflict-resolution policies (e.g., humanitarian aid, reparations, political compromise). Measured on a Likert scale, participants will indicate their agreement with statements about these policies (e.g., "I support providing humanitarian aid to outgroup members").

2. Measured Predictors:

- Personal Emotions: Six group-based emotions (hate, anger, fear, empathy, guilt, and hope) toward the outgroup. Participants will rate their personal experience of these emotions using a Likert scale (e.g., "I feel anger about the actions of outgroup in the context of the conflict.").

- Emotion Norms: Perceived descriptive and prescriptive emotion norms. Descriptive norms measure the perceived prevalence of each emotion within participants' groups (e.g., "How many people in your group feel empathy (compassion) for the suffering of outgroup members in the context of the conflict.?"). Prescriptive norms measure the perceived desirability of emotions (e.g., "How many people think it is justified to feel anger about the actions of outgroup in the context of the conflict?").

3. Covariates:

- Socio-demographics (Age, gender, education level, economic status, religious views, place of residence)
  
- Group Identification: Participants' level of identification with their group (e.g., ethnonational, religious, or political group). This is measured with items assessing how strongly they feel attached to the group (e.g., "Being a member of the ingroup is an important part of my identity").

- Other Social Norms: Additional control measures for other types of social norms, such as norms around intergroup contact, reconciliation and trust.
table.indices: Some variables will be combined by taking the mean to form indices, such as identity scales and intergroup contact norms. Before combining these items into an index, we will conduct a reliability analysis (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) to ensure internal consistency. Only variables with acceptable reliability (typically, an alpha of 0.70 or higher) will be summed to form the index. If reliability is lower, we will re-evaluate the items and consider excluding poorly performing items before combining them. The final index will represent the average score across the included items for each participant.
table.statistical_tests:
H1, H2, H3 & H3.1
Multiple regression for mediation analysis will be used to assess direct and indirect effects of emotion norms (independent variable)  on support for conflict-related policies (dependent variable) via personal emotions (mediator). Separate models will be run for each emotion and emotion norm, as well as a single model with all emotions and emotion norms to assess their relative effects. Socio-demographic controls will be included. 

H4: Misperceptions of norms and policy support
Multiple regression will test whether misperceptions of norms (calculated as the difference between perceived and actual norms) predict support for conflict-related policies (dependent variable). Control variables such as countries, socio-demographics and personal emotions will be included.

H5: Moderation by group identification
Moderation analysis using multiple regression will assess the interaction between emotion norms and group identification to predict support for conflict-related policies. The interaction term between emotion norms and group identification will test whether the relationship between emotion norms and policy support varies depending on the level of group identification. Socio-demographics and personal emotions will be included as control variables.

H6: Reference groups
Multiple regressions, as described under H3, will be used to asses direct effects emotion norms on support for conflict-related policies (dependent variable). Separate models will be run for each emotion norm within each reference group. In addition, combined models including emotion norms from all three reference groups (e.g., national hate norm, political hate norm, and local hate norm) will be estimated to evaluate their relative influence.

In H1 to H6: 
Subgroup analyses will be conducted for each country and for distinct conflict groups (where applicable), such as Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland. Separate models will be run to estimate the relationships between variables across different groups and countries.

H7: Cross-country differences

To test H7, we aim to assess whether the strength of the association between perceived emotion norms and support for conflict-related policies varies systematically by country-level conflict status (ongoing vs. post-conflict). Given our cross-national sample includes 13 countries, we will use two complementary strategies to analyse this relationship while accounting for the nested data structure and the small number of level-2 units.

1. Two-Step Estimation Approach 

We will adopt a two-step estimation procedure as our primary strategy, given its transparency and its appropriateness for settings with a small number of countries and a large number of respondents per country:

 Step 1: For each country, we will estimate the individual-level association between perceived emotion norms and policy support using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. These models will control for relevant individual-level covariates.

 Step 2: We will extract the estimated regression coefficients for the effect of perceived emotion norms on policy support from each country-level model. These coefficients will then be used as dependent variables in a country-level linear regression, with the binary indicator of conflict stage (0 = post-conflict, 1 = ongoing conflict) as the independent variable.

This will allow us to test whether the association between emotion norms and policy support is significantly stronger in ongoing conflict countries than in post-conflict countries, as predicted in H6.

We acknowledge that, due to the limited number of countries (N = 13), this second-stage analysis will have limited statistical power, and results will be interpreted cautiously.

2. Multilevel Modeling 

As a robustness check, we will also explore multilevel models (hierarchical linear models) that include random intercepts for countries, and random slopes for the emotion norms predictor. In these models, we will test for cross-level interactions between perceived emotion norms (level-1 predictor) and country-level conflict stage (level-2 moderator). Specifically, a significant cross-level interaction between perceived emotion norms and conflict stage would support H6, indicating that the strength of the association varies by national context.

We are aware of concerns about the stability of random effect estimates with only 13 countries. Following Gelman & Hill (2007), we will not dismiss multilevel models a priori but will interpret them with caution and focus on them as supplementary to the two-step approach.

H8: Competitive victimhood and outgroup responsibility
Multiple regression will be used to test whether competitive victimhood beliefs and higher attribution of responsibility to the outgroup predict greater support for conflict-promoting policies. Control variables will include socio-demographics, country, and personal emotions.

H9: Inclusive victimhood and ingroup responsibility
Multiple regression will assess whether inclusive victimhood beliefs and greater recognition of ingroup responsibility predict higher support for conflict-resolution policies. Socio-demographics, country, and personal emotions will be included as controls.

H10: Historical lesson framing
Separate regressions will test whether framing group victimization as a lesson to avoid harm predicts support for reconciliation policies, and whether framing it as a justification for self-defense predicts support for conflict-promoting policies. Control variables will include socio-demographics, emotions, and victimhood beliefs.

H11: Interaction between victimhood beliefs and historical lesson framing
Moderation analysis using regression will test interactions between inclusive victimhood and "avoid harm" framing, and between competitive victimhood and "self-defense" framing, in predicting policy support. Controls will include socio-demographics, emotions, and country fixed effects.

For H8 to H11, we will also conduct subgroup analyses by country and conflict group (where applicable) to explore whether effects are consistent across contexts.
table.research_questions:
H1: Perceived emotion norms will be positively associated with corresponding personal emotions. For example, individuals who perceive stronger group norms of empathy will express higher personal levels of empathy.

H2: Perceived emotion norms will be positively associated with support for relevant conflict-related policies. Specifically, stronger perceived norms of constructive intergroup emotions (e.g., empathy) will be associated with greater support for conflict-moderating policies, whereas stronger perceived norms of negative intergroup emotions (e.g., hate) will be associated with greater support for conflict-promoting policies.

H3: The effect of perceived emotion norms on support for conflict-related policies will be mediated by personal emotions.

H3.1: Perceived emotion norms will have a direct effect on support for conflict-related policies, even when controlling for corresponding personal emotions. That is, perceived norms will have an additional direct (un-mediated, or mediated otherwise) on policy support.

H4: Group identification will moderate the relationship between perceived emotion norms and policy support. The association between emotion norms and policy support will be stronger among individuals with higher levels of group identification compared to those with lower identification.

H5: Misperceptions of emotion norms will be associated with support for conflict-related policies. Specifically, individuals who underestimate the prevalence of positive emotion norms (e.g., empathy) within their group will show lower support for conflict-moderating policies, whereas individuals who overestimate the prevalence of negative emotion norms (e.g., hate) will show greater support for conflict-promoting policies.
We expect that individuals will often misperceive the prevalence of group emotions, though the direction and magnitude of these misperceptions are likely to vary. We will explore whether these misperceptions depend on the specific emotion, individual characteristics, and country-level context.

H6: Importance of Reference Groups
Social norms are most influential when they are linked to reference groups - groups to which people belong to and care about (Sherif & Sherif, 1964). In conflict settings, research often focuses on norms within conflict-defined groups (e.g., ethnic or national groups), as violent conflict tends to heighten identification with these groups, making them chronically salient lenses through which individuals interpret the conflict and related issues (Elcheroth & Reicher, 2017). However, other reference groups - such as political groups (Harel, Maoz, & Halperin, 2020) or local community groups (e.g., neighbors, friends; Matthes et al., 2018) - can also play a key role.
In a pilot study conducted in Israel (Penić, Mostovoy, & Halperin, 2024), we found that perceived emotion norms within one’s political group were more predictive of policy support than those within the broader national group. This suggests that the relative influence of reference groups may vary by context.
In this study, we will assess the influence of perceived emotion norms across three types of reference groups:
1.	Conflict-defined group (e.g., ethnic or national group central to the conflict),
2.	Political group (e.g., based on ideological alignment such as left vs. right),
3.	Local community group (e.g., village, town, or neighborhood).
Hypotheses:
•	H6.1: Perceived emotion norms in the conflict-defined group will be positively associated with personal emotions and support for conflict-related policies, in line with the mediation and direct effect patterns described in H1–H5.
•	H6.2: Perceived emotion norms in the political group and local community group will also show positive associations with personal emotions and policy support, consistent with the relationships outlined in H1–H5. However, the relative influence of these groups is expected to vary across reference groups and countries.
Specifically, in Israel, we expect political group norms to be the most influential predictor of personal emotions and policy support. In other countries, we do not formulate specific predictions regarding which reference group will be most influential, and will examine these differences in an exploratory manner.

H7: The relationship between emotion norms and policy support will differ across national contexts. Specifically, the association will be stronger in countries experiencing ongoing conflict compared to countries in a post-conflict phase.

H8: Embracing a competitive victimhood belief, in addition to higher attribution of responsibility to the outgroup, will predict support for conflict-promoting policies. 

H9: Embracing an inclusive victimhood belief, in addition to higher recognition of the ingroup responsibility, will predict support for conflict-resolution policies.

H10: Those who perceive the history of their group’s victimization as a lesson to avoid perpetuating harm to others will show greater support for reconciliation-oriented policies. Conversely, those who interpret their group’s history as a justification for self-defense, including violence if necessary, will exhibit higher support for conflict-promoting policies.

H11: The relationship between victimhood narratives (inclusive vs. competitive) and policy support (reconciliation vs. conflict) will be moderated by perceptions of historical lessons, such that inclusive victimhood combined with a commitment to avoid harm will amplify support for reconciliation-related policies. In contrast, competitive victimhood combined with a focus on self-defense will increase support for conflict-related policies.

Collective victimization can have different political consequences.

Experiences of war, persecution, occupation, and intergroup violence may contribute to defensive or hostile orientations toward other groups, but they may also foster recognition of shared suffering and support for more constructive intergroup relations (Vollhardt & Bilali, 2015; Vollhardt, Cohrs, et al., 2021).

text.text: Research on collective victimhood distinguishes the experience of harm from the beliefs through which group members interpret that harm (Bar-Tal et al., 2009; Noor et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Research on collective victimhood distinguishes the experience of harm from the beliefs through which group members interpret that harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bar-Tal et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Noor et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Some beliefs compare an ingroup's suffering with that of an adversary or other groups; others connect the ingroup's experience to the victimization of others (Noor et al., 2017; Vollhardt, 2015).
text.formatted: Some beliefs compare an ingroup's suffering with that of an adversary or other groups; others connect the ingroup's experience to the victimization of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Noor et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Vollhardt, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Recognizing victims across group boundaries can involve acknowledging comparable suffering or recognizing their shared humanity despite differences in the extent of harm.
These understandings of collective suffering may carry distinct implications for reconciliation, intergroup equality, and aggression.
Within this literature, two competitive beliefs concern suffering relative to a particular conflict opponent or relative to groups worldwide.

Two inclusive beliefs make a different distinction: perceiving parity in the suffering of the ingroup and its adversary versus recognizing the shared human standing of victims even where their experiences differ.
The latter, which we call human-level inclusive victimhood, acknowledges victimization across group boundaries independently of judgments about the relative magnitude of suffering.

The present study examines these four victimhood beliefs and their associations with three conflict-related outcomes: support for reconciliation policies, support for intergroup-equality policies, and aggression endorsement or justification.
Examining these beliefs separately advances our understanding of variation within competitive and inclusive victimhood.

A central contribution is the distinction between comparative and human-level inclusive victimhood and the examination of their respective associations with conflict-related policy support and aggression.
A second contribution concerns variation across conflict contexts.

Drawing on survey data from 14 ethnonational groups in 10 conflict-affected settings, we investigate differences in the endorsement and political associations of victimhood beliefs across groups and explore the relevance of conflict stage and relative group power.

Together, these contributions extend research on collective victimhood by examining how the content of beliefs about suffering and the contexts in which they are held relate to conflict-related responses.
Collective victimhood refers to a shared understanding of harm as unjust, undeserved, and consequential for the group.

In intractable conflicts, this understanding can become embedded in collective memory and the broader ethos of conflict, shaping how group members interpret their past and present circumstances (Bar-Tal et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In intractable conflicts, this understanding can become embedded in collective memory and the broader ethos of conflict, shaping how group members interpret their past and present circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bar-Tal et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals may participate in collective narratives of victimization without having personally experienced the events invoked by those narratives, and similar histories of harm may be interpreted through different comparative frameworks (Noor et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Individuals may participate in collective narratives of victimization without having personally experienced the events invoked by those narratives, and similar histories of harm may be interpreted through different comparative frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Noor et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The social and political meanings attributed to suffering are central to these interpretations. Bilali and Vollhardt (2019) show that groups involved in collective violence may disagree about who was victimized, who was responsible, perpetrators' intentions, the severity of harm, and the historical period considered relevant.

text.text: Their account distinguishes motivations to protect the group and obtain acknowledgment from motivations to defend the ingroup's moral image.
Research on the Lebanese Civil War further illustrates these dynamics.

text.text: At the same time, participants acknowledged outgroup suffering, illustrating how recognition of another group's victimhood can coexist with defensive interpretations of the conflict.
These perspectives highlight how interpretations of collective victimization are embedded in broader understandings of group identity, responsibility, and conflict history.
They also suggest that the political associations of victimhood beliefs may differ according to how the ingroup's suffering is understood in relation to that of others.
Competitive victimhood concerns the belief that the ingroup has suffered more than another group (Noor et al., 2012).

text.text: We distinguish two competitive beliefs.
Conflict-specific competitive victimhood concerns the judgment that the ingroup suffered more harm than the focal adversary during the conflict.
Global competitive victimhood concerns the broader claim that no group anywhere has experienced as much victimization as the ingroup.

These formulations differ in their comparison referents and in the scope of the claims they make (Vollhardt, Cohrs, et al., 2021; Vollhardt, Szabó, et al., 2021). Noor et al. (2012) conceptualize competitive victimhood as an intergroup competition that can obstruct forgiveness and peaceful conflict resolution.

text.text: Their account connects competition over victim status to broader intergroup rivalry and, drawing on the needs-based model (Shnabel & Nadler, 2008), proposes that such competition may serve motivations to restore power or moral acceptance.

text.text: Both competitive beliefs may accompany aggression by placing victimhood within competition over legitimacy, recognition, and moral standing.
However, the comparison referent may shape the political relevance of these claims.

Conflict-specific competitive victimhood is embedded in a particular adversarial relationship and may be especially relevant to judgments about the opponent's responsibility, legitimacy, and entitlement to reconciliation or equal treatment.
Global competitive victimhood extends beyond the immediate conflict, locating the ingroup within a broader hierarchy of suffering and potentially reinforcing claims of exceptional victimization.
Their political associations may therefore differ across groups and conflict settings (Noor et al., 2017; Vollhardt, Szabó, et al., 2021).

In a multigroup study of Armenian Americans, Jewish Americans, Hungarians, and Poles, Vollhardt, Cohrs, et al. (2021) examined exclusive comparative victim beliefs using global or regional victim-group comparisons and linked these beliefs to hostile intergroup outcomes.

(2021)</ref> examined exclusive comparative victim beliefs using global or regional victim-group comparisons and linked these beliefs to hostile intergroup outcomes.

text.text: Building on this research, the present study examines the distinct associations of conflict-specific and global competitive victimhood alongside two forms of inclusive victimhood across multiple conflict contexts.
Inclusive victimhood connects the ingroup's suffering to that of others, extending recognition of victimization across group boundaries (Vollhardt, 2015).
text.formatted: Inclusive victimhood connects the ingroup's suffering to that of others, extending recognition of victimization across group boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Vollhardt, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Research has generally associated inclusive victimhood with constructive intergroup attitudes, including prosocial orientations, willingness for contact, and support for peace (Noor et al., 2015; Voca et al., 2023; Vollhardt & Bilali, 2015).
text.formatted: Research has generally associated inclusive victimhood with constructive intergroup attitudes, including prosocial orientations, willingness for contact, and support for peace <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Noor et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Voca et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Vollhardt & Bilali, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A recent meta-analysis of 745 estimates from 103 articles similarly found that inclusive victimhood beliefs tended to be associated with more constructive intergroup outcomes, whereas non-inclusive beliefs were generally associated with conflictenhancing attitudes (Kljajić et al., 2026).

(2022) differentiated general inclusion, involving victim groups worldwide, from conflict-specific inclusion involving opposing groups. Cohrs et al. (2015) further distinguished universal from selective interpretations of shared suffering, showing that their implications for forgiveness differed.

text.text: The present study examines a complementary distinction: whether recognizing an adversary's victimhood requires perceiving equivalent suffering or instead involves acknowledging victims' shared human standing despite differences in victimization.
Parity-based conflict-specific inclusive victimhood involves the judgment that the ingroup suffered as much harm as its focal adversary during the conflict.
Human-level inclusive victimhood, by contrast, involves recognizing that a victim is a victim at the basic human level, regardless of group membership or differences in the extent of harm.
This recognition remains situated within the relationship between conflict opponents, distinguishing it from broader identification with all humanity (McFarland et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This recognition remains situated within the relationship between conflict opponents, distinguishing it from broader identification with all humanity <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(McFarland et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is particularly relevant in conflicts characterized by asymmetrical suffering or contested historical narratives.
Individuals may acknowledge an adversary's victimization without considering the groups' suffering equivalent.
Human-level inclusion accommodates such recognition, whereas parity-based inclusion rests on a comparative judgment about the magnitude of harm.
These different understandings of shared victimhood may have distinct political implications, particularly for support for reconciliation and intergroup equality.
Victimhood beliefs emerge within specific histories of violence, distributions of power, interpretations of responsibility, and public narratives of conflict (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019).
text.formatted: Victimhood beliefs emerge within specific histories of violence, distributions of power, interpretations of responsibility, and public narratives of conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Their endorsement and associations with conflict-related outcomes may consequently vary across ethnonational groups and conflict settings.
The same belief may carry different political meanings depending on the groups involved, their experiences of victimization, and the role of collective suffering in contemporary intergroup relations.
Examining group-specific patterns alongside pooled associations can reveal both recurring relationships and differences in how victimhood beliefs relate to conflict-related responses.
Previous research illustrates the importance of these contextual meanings.

In Northern Ireland, Cohrs et al. (2015) showed that the relationship between inclusive victimhood and forgiveness depended on how similarities in suffering were understood. Rupar et al. (2022) likewise documented differences in the associations between inclusive victimhood and willingness for different forms of intergroup contact in Bosnian and Basque samples.

text.text: Beyond individual-level beliefs, research on Croatia and Kosovo has shown how narratives of national victimization, liberation, and victory remain closely connected to state legitimacy and political identity after the end of armed violence (Boduszyński & Pavlaković, 2019).

text.text: These findings illustrate how the meaning and political relevance of collective suffering are embedded in particular historical and political contexts.
Two contextual characteristics may be especially relevant to variation in the associations between victimhood beliefs and conflict-related outcomes.
First, conflict stage may shape the salience and interpretation of collective victimization.
Ongoing conflicts involve immediate insecurity, mobilization, and perceived threat, potentially intensifying competition over victimhood and distinctions between victims and perpetrators.

Post-conflict settings may provide different opportunities for coexistence and the reinterpretation of collective narratives, while memories of violence and disputes over responsibility can continue to shape intergroup relations.
Such differences may also shape the political associations of victimhood beliefs.
Second, relative group power may influence the meanings attached to victimhood claims and their political implications.

Members of relatively disadvantaged groups may invoke collective suffering in demands for acknowledgment, protection, and equal treatment, whereas members of relatively advantaged groups may draw on victimhood narratives to affirm their group's moral standing or defend existing arrangements (Kahalon et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Members of relatively disadvantaged groups may invoke collective suffering in demands for acknowledgment, protection, and equal treatment, whereas members of relatively advantaged groups may draw on victimhood narratives to affirm their group's moral standing or defend existing arrangements <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kahalon et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These dynamics are particularly relevant to comparative victimhood beliefs, as claims about relative suffering are embedded in relationships characterized by different distributions of power, experiences of violence, and access to recognition.
Group positions may also change over time, making the distinction between power during the focal conflict and power at the time of the survey theoretically relevant.
The comparative design allows us to address two related questions about contextual variation.

The first concerns between-group heterogeneity: the extent to which associations between victimhood beliefs and conflict-related outcomes are similar across groups or differ in magnitude and direction.
The second concerns contextual influences on this heterogeneity, particularly whether conflict stage and dyad-specific relative power are associated with differences in these relationships.

By combining group-specific analyses with exploratory contextual comparisons, we examine how the political associations of collective victimhood vary across conflict-affected societies and identify patterns that may inform the interpretation of these differences.
The political implications of victimhood beliefs may differ across the outcomes being considered.
We examine three domains: reconciliation-policy support, intergroup-equality-policy support, and aggression endorsement or justification.
Reconciliation concerns support for peaceful coexistence, dialogue, negotiation, or renewed intergroup relations.
Intergroup equality concerns support for policies promoting equal treatment, representation, or opportunities between groups, including where such policies may challenge established group advantages.

Aggression concerns the endorsement or justification of violent or aggressive action against an outgroup in connection with conflict goals, including aggression-related policies where these are represented in the measures.
Although related, these outcomes involve different political judgments.
Support for improved relations with an adversary does not necessarily imply endorsement of policies that change the distribution of rights or opportunities between groups.
Similarly, rejecting aggression does not necessarily entail support for either reconciliation or equality.
Because competitive and inclusive victimhood beliefs differ in their comparison referents and the forms of recognition they express, their associations may also vary across these political domains.
Distinguishing the outcomes therefore allows us to examine how different interpretations of collective suffering relate to specific responses to intergroup conflict.

The present study examines associations between four collective victimhood beliefs and three conflict-related outcomes among 12,499 respondents from 14 ethnonational groups across VICTIMHOOD AND POLICY SUPPORT 11 10 conflict-affected settings.
The four victimhood beliefs are entered simultaneously in the primary models, allowing us to estimate their distinct associations while accounting for their overlap.

Drawing on previous research linking competitive victimhood to conflict-enhancing responses and inclusive victimhood to constructive intergroup attitudes (Adelman et al., 2016; Kljajić et al., 2026; Noor et al., 2012; Vollhardt & Bilali, 2015), we formulated two directional hypotheses, preregistered as part of the broader project (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/JAEMS).

text.text: All four indicators were analyzed separately and included simultaneously in the focal regression models.
Three outcomes were examined: reconciliation-policy support, intergroup-equality-policy support, and aggression endorsement or justification.

text.text: Intergroup equality was assessed with "I would support policies that promote equality between the groups in housing, education and jobs", supplemented where available by an item concerning locally relevant equal treatment, resource distribution, or representation.

Aggression was assessed with a general item concerning the acceptability of violence against the outgroup in pursuit of ingroup conflict goals and, where administered, a settingspecific item on aggressive action or policy.
In ongoing-conflict settings, the general item was "Physical and violent actions against the members of the outgroup are justified in order to promote our goals in the conflict".

In post-conflict settings, the general item referred to the justification of violence during the past conflict, whereas the setting-specific item referred to aggression in a possible renewed conflict.
The outcome therefore captures aggression endorsement or justification, with differences in temporal framing across settings.
Outcome scores were calculated as the mean of available general and setting-specific items; a single available item constituted the score when no second item was retained.
For intergroup equality in both Thai groups, only the general item was used because its association with the setting-specific item was negligible or negative.
The setting-specific aggression item was not administered in Turkey or either Indian group.
Accordingly, outcomes were based on one or two items depending on the setting.

The present study examined how four collective victimhood beliefs relate to reconciliation, intergroup equality, and aggression-related policy support across 14 ethnonational groups in 10 conflict-affected societies.

Both conflict-specific and global competitive victimhood were positively associated with aggression-related policy support, whereas both forms of inclusive victimhood were positively associated with reconciliation and equality.
Beyond these preregistered associations, the findings highlight differences within each family of beliefs.
Human-level inclusive victimhood showed stronger positive associations with reconciliation and equality and a more negative association with aggression than parity-based inclusion.
Global competitive victimhood also showed more consistent associations across groups than conflictspecific competitive victimhood.

These patterns suggest that the political relevance of collective victimhood depends not only on whether a belief is competitive or inclusive, but also on what kind of comparison or recognition it expresses.
The clearest theoretical distinction concerns two ways of recognizing victimization across group boundaries.
Parity-based inclusive victimhood entails a judgment that the ingroup and its conflict opponent suffered comparably.
Human-level inclusive victimhood instead affirms victims' shared human standing while explicitly allowing differences in their experiences of victimization.
Recognizing another group's suffering in this way need not entail agreement about the relative magnitude of harm.

This distinction is particularly relevant where accounts of victimization are asymmetric or contested: acknowledgment of an adversary's suffering can be conceptually separated from claims that the two groups suffered equally.
The empirical patterns corresponded to this distinction.

Human-level inclusive victimhood was more strongly associated with reconciliation and equality policy support than parity-based inclusion, and its association with aggression-related policy support was negative across all 14 groups.
Parity-based inclusion showed smaller positive pooled associations with reconciliation and equality, greater variation across groups, and no pooled association with aggression.

These findings extend research linking inclusive victim consciousness to constructive intergroup orientations (Vollhardt & Bilali, 2015) by distinguishing recognition of another group's victimhood from a judgment of equivalent suffering.
text.formatted: These findings extend research linking inclusive victim consciousness to constructive intergroup orientations <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Vollhardt & Bilali, 2015)</ref> by distinguishing recognition of another group's victimhood from a judgment of equivalent suffering.

text.text: They also complement work on different referents and interpretations of inclusive victimhood (Cohrs et al., 2015; Rupar et al., 2022).
text.formatted: They also complement work on different referents and interpretations of inclusive victimhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cohrs et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Rupar et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction has implications for the political outcomes examined here.
Support for peaceful coexistence does not necessarily entail support for equal treatment, opportunities, or representation.

Yet human-level inclusion was associated with both reconciliation and equality, suggesting that recognizing victims across group boundaries may be relevant not only to intergroup relations but also to judgments about how groups should be treated politically.
Its negative association with aggression further distinguishes it from parity-based inclusion.
One possible interpretation is that acknowledging common human standing provides a basis for political consideration of an adversary without requiring agreement about whose suffering was greater.

This interpretation is related to work on identification with all humanity and equal concern for ingroup and outgroup members (McFarland et al., 2012), although the belief examined here is specifically anchored in experiences of victimization rather than humanity as a general identity.
text.formatted: This interpretation is related to work on identification with all humanity and equal concern for ingroup and outgroup members <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(McFarland et al., 2012)</ref>, although the belief examined here is specifically anchored in experiences of victimization rather than humanity as a general identity.

text.text: The two competitive beliefs also showed distinct patterns.

Global competitive victimhood, expressed as a claim that no other group has suffered as much as the ingroup, was positively associated with aggression-related policy support and negatively associated with reconciliation and equality in most groups.
This pattern is consistent with research connecting competitive and non-inclusive victimhood to conflict-enhancing intergroup orientations (Noor et al., 2012; Kljajić et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with research connecting competitive and non-inclusive victimhood to conflict-enhancing intergroup orientations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Noor et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kljajić et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A claim of exceptional suffering that extends beyond the immediate adversarial relationship may accompany a broader understanding of the ingroup as uniquely entitled to recognition or protection, with implications for judgments about accommodation and equality.

Conflict-specific competitive victimhood also showed positive pooled associations with aggression, but its associations with reconciliation and equality varied more substantially across groups, including differences in direction.

Comparisons with a particular opponent may be especially sensitive to how the parties interpret the focal conflict, assign responsibility, and situate their respective experiences within collective narratives (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019).
text.formatted: Comparisons with a particular opponent may be especially sensitive to how the parties interpret the focal conflict, assign responsibility, and situate their respective experiences within collective narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the global item expresses an especially strong claim of exceptional suffering.
The two indicators thus differ in wording and claim strength as well as comparison referent, which is relevant when interpreting their contrasting patterns.
Together, the findings support examining the substantive content of competitive beliefs rather than treating competitive victimhood as a uniform orientation.
The associations between victimhood beliefs and policy support varied in magnitude across ethnonational groups, even when their directions were similar.

This heterogeneity is compatible with the view that beliefs about collective suffering acquire meaning within particular histories of violence, political relationships, and narratives of responsibility (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019).
text.formatted: This heterogeneity is compatible with the view that beliefs about collective suffering acquire meaning within particular histories of violence, political relationships, and narratives of responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The group profiles illustrate this contextual variation.

Ukrainian respondents reported relatively high conflict-specific competitive victimhood and low parity-based inclusion during the full-scale war with Russia, a setting in which comparisons with the adversary take place amid ongoing violence.
Wartime narratives and judgments about territorial concessions provide relevant background for interpreting such comparisons (Bachleitner, 2025).
text.formatted: Wartime narratives and judgments about territorial concessions provide relevant background for interpreting such comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bachleitner, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Relatively high competitive and low parity-based inclusion also appeared among Kosovo Albanians, Bosniaks in Bosnia, and Croats, suggesting that adversarial comparisons can remain salient after armed conflict has ended.
Historical narratives of victimization, victory, and responsibility remain relevant to political identities in these settings (Boduszyński & Pavlaković, 2019; Demirel, 2023).

text.text: Southern Thailand offered a different descriptive pattern: both Malay Muslim and Thai Buddhist samples had relatively high group means on conflict-specific competitive and inclusive victimhood.

The region's history of ethno-religious conflict and intercommunal coexistence provides a context in which acknowledgment of ingroup and outgroup suffering may both be salient (Askew, 2009; Mohamad, 2018).
text.formatted: The region's history of ethno-religious conflict and intercommunal coexistence provides a context in which acknowledgment of ingroup and outgroup suffering may both be salient <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Askew, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Mohamad, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These aggregate patterns suggest that relatively high levels of competitive and inclusive beliefs can be observed in the same populations; they do not establish that individual respondents endorsed both.
Across the examples, differences in sampling and measurement also limit direct comparisons of group levels.
Their principal value is to illustrate variation in how the beliefs are expressed across settings.
Exploratory contextual analyses offered more specific, though necessarily limited, evidence about this variation.

The association between human-level inclusive victimhood and equality-policy support was weaker in settings classified as active-conflict than in those classified as post-conflict, a difference also observed in the complementary two-stage analysis.
One possibility is that immediate security concerns and adversarial political demands affect how recognition of another group's suffering relates to support for equality-oriented policies.
The corresponding moderation of reconciliation was not statistically reliable, however, and the active-conflict category included diverse patterns.

The findings therefore point to a potentially relevant distinction between recognizing shared humanity and supporting equality under different conflict conditions, rather than to a uniform contextual effect.
Relative group power was also relevant to one exploratory association.

Conflict-specific competitive victimhood was more negatively associated with equality-policy support among groups classified as relatively higher-power during the focal conflict than among lower-power groups.
This contrast survived multiplicity adjustment in the individual-level moderation analysis; the two-stage estimate pointed in the same direction but did not survive that adjustment.

The pattern is compatible with the possibility that claims of greater ingroup suffering carry different political implications when they are expressed from positions of relative advantage or disadvantage, particularly for policies concerning intergroup equality.
The evidence is exploratory, and power was classified using context-specific indicators that were not fully equivalent across conflicts.
Other contextual comparisons offered less consistent evidence, leaving the sources of much between-group heterogeneity to be examined in future research.
Additional analyses of conflict duration yielded no clear moderation by cumulative conflict years.

The more positive human-level inclusion-equality association at higher values of peace years was consistent with the conflict-stage contrast, but the two findings are not independent: peace years was zero in all active-conflict settings.
The analyses therefore cannot establish that elapsed time since conflict cessation, rather than other differences between settings, accounts for the association.
These exploratory patterns merit examination in a larger sample of conflict contexts.
A strength of this study is its examination of distinct victimhood beliefs and political outcomes across multiple conflict-affected populations within a common analytic framework.
Considering reconciliation, equality, and aggression-related policy support separately revealed differences that would be obscured by a single index of constructive or conflict-enhancing attitudes.
The combination of pooled and group-specific analyses also made it possible to identify recurring associations while examining how their magnitudes varied across groups.
Several limitations qualify these contributions.

The cross-sectional design does not establish whether victimhood beliefs shape policy support, whether political orientations inform beliefs about suffering, or whether both reflect other psychological and contextual processes.
Longitudinal and experimental studies could investigate changes in these relationships and test the effects of victimhood framings on political judgments.
In addition, each victimhood belief was represented by a single item.
The indicators differ not only in comparison referent but also in wording, the strength of their claims, and moral content.
In particular, the human-level item combines recognition of victimization with an explicit appeal to shared humanity.
Matched multi-item measures would help determine which of these features account for the observed differences in associations.
The conflict-related outcomes were conceptually harmonized but not identically composed in every setting.
Some relied on one item and others on two; the aggression items also differed in temporal framing between active-and post-conflict settings.
Data were collected predominantly through nonprobability online panels, whereas southern Thailand used face-toface interviews.
Together with the absence of established measurement invariance, these features constrain interpretations of cross-group mean differences and population-level generalization.
Moreover, the study measured expressed policy support and aggression endorsement or justification, not observed political behavior.
Future research could assess whether the distinctions extend to actual cooperation, collective action, voting, or responses to specific institutional reforms.
Finally, the contextual analyses drew on 14 ethnonational groups in 10 conflict settings, limiting precision at the level where conflict stage and relative power were classified.
The power coding combined evidence about institutional access, wartime advantage, and interstate capabilities according to the focal dyad.
Studies involving more conflict settings, independently evaluated classifications, and alternative indicators of power would allow stronger tests of contextual explanations.
Such work would be especially informative if it examined how perceived asymmetries in suffering and responsibility intersect with structural power in shaping support for equality and reconciliation.
Collective victimhood beliefs were associated with distinct patterns of support for reconciliation, intergroup equality, and aggression-related policies across conflict-affected societies.
The central contribution is the distinction between perceiving parity in the suffering of opposing groups and recognizing victims' shared human standing despite differences in their experiences.
The latter showed stronger and more consistent associations with reconciliation and equality, alongside a negative association with aggression-related policy support.
Within competitive victimhood, the scope and content of suffering comparisons also mattered.
Understanding these distinctions offers a more differentiated account of how interpretations of collective harm relate to political responses in conflict-affected societies.

Cumulative conflict years was defined as the number of distinct calendar years between 1946 and 2024 in which at least one state-based armed conflict was recorded for the setting, counting each year only once regardless of the number of recorded conflicts.

Peace years was calculated as the number of years elapsed since the most recent recorded conflict year (2024 minus the last conflict year), with a value of zero assigned to settings experiencing recorded conflict in 2024.
